title: Güler’s brilliance can be key in battle with USMNT for World Cup Group D supremacy
content:
Head coach Vincenzo Montella believes the youthful brilliance of Arda Güler can give Turkey a crucial edge against World Cup co-host the United States and the rest of a tightly matched Group D.

Güler, the 21-year-old Real Madrid midfielder, along with Juventus forward Kenan Yıldız and Inter Milan captain Hakan Çalhanoğlu, leads a Turkey side that many expect to form the biggest group-stage threat to the USMNT. They will meet in their third matches, on June 25 in Los Angeles.

Speaking from the Turkish national team’s training camp in Fort Lauderdale before the squad’s friendly against Venezuela on Saturday, Montella said no team should be taken lightly, with Paraguay and Australia making up the rest of the group.

“I can say that it is a group made up of teams that are fairly close in quality to one another,” Montella said. “You should never underestimate any group or any opponent. That’s why we must approach it with that awareness.”

The spotlight will land on Güler, who will be the face of a squad carrying the country’s highest expectations since its third-place finish at the 2002 World Cup.

Montella believes his dynamic playmaker is only just beginning to realize his potential.

“When you play for Real Madrid, there is no thought other than winning,” Montella said. “That mindset develops you mentally. He is still very young and a player with tremendous room for growth, and we are ready to support that development here as well.”

After lifting La Liga and the Champions League early in his career, Güler has an opportunity to make himself a national hero.

Montella pointed to the unique education Güler has received in Madrid, where success is expected every season and failure is scrutinized just as intensely.

“At Real Madrid, he has already experienced many different situations,” Montella said. “He has won the Champions League and the league title. He has also experienced seasons in which they did not win the Champions League and seasons in which they did not win the league.”

Those experiences, Montella argued, are shaping Güler into a more complete player.

“He has gone through every kind of experience and seen those environments firsthand,” Montella said. “All of that helps him grow mentally, and it also improves his game.”

Güler will wear the No. 8 jersey at the World Cup, the same number worn by legendary midfielder Tugay Kerimoğlu during the country’s unforgettable run to the semi-finals in 2002.

“I am proud to wear his number,” Güler said. “I am living my dream and will do anything to bring the same success to our country as they did.”

While Turkish supporters view Güler as the player best positioned to help Turkey overcome a tricky set of group opponents, Montella has stressed throughout the camp that collective discipline and respect for every foe will determine how far his team advances.

“I can say that it is a group made up of teams that are fairly close in quality to one another,” Montella said. “You should never underestimate any group or any opponent. That’s why we must approach it with that awareness.”

The United States has the benefit of home support, Australia enters the competition with extensive experience in modern World Cups, and Paraguay arrives after a strong qualifying campaign in South America.

For a country making its first World Cup appearance in nearly a quarter century, the emergence of Güler has fueled hopes that this squad could achieve something special on the global stage.

Montella, however, appears focused less on the hype and more on the process. “There is never such a thing as an easy game in football,” he said.
